ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: People described as unable to see, hear, and speak.
EvidenceBody: In the Chan record, the full phrase becomes the stable wording of Xuansha Shibei's “three kinds of invalids” public case. Xuansha asks how one receives people who cannot see a raised mallet or whisk, hear spoken command, or answer. Yuanwu Keqin warns his audience against treating his discussion as nothing more than the disability list, then asks where the blind, deaf, and mute fellow stands; Xuedou Chongxian begins his verse with the same phrase. In a Yunmen case, Yunmen tests an unnamed monk for deafness and muteness, and Xuedou applies the full phrase to him. Yuelin Shiguan later labels and re-asks Xuansha's case. Guting Shanjian also compares people unable to resolve doubt with the blind, deaf, and mute. Zen bends a literal description into repeatable wording for a public case and an interview about receiving people when visible, audible, and spoken exchange fails; the entry does not invent a diagnosis beyond each recorded deployment.

DraftEvidence.ZenBend: For 盲聾瘖啞, the stored cases establish this term-specific deployment: People described as unable to see, hear, and speak.
DraftEvidence.CounterexampleOrLimit: The literal comparison and the named case still point to people described by the same disabilities, so item 8 does not warrant a split. Different readings of why Yuanwu warns against a merely literal handling are not separate things and are not supplied here.
